newsitem.title: UK: Arms protesters raise hackles at BAe meeting.
newsitem.headline: Arms protesters raise hackles at BAe meeting.

text.p: British Aerospace Plc's traditionally rumbustious shareholders' meeting ended peacefully after nearly three hours of disruptive questioning from arms trade protesters on Wednesday.
Last year the meeting was hurriedly closed after peace campaigners sent directors scurrying for cover with a volley of eggs.
This year fortifications had been improved with directors keeping their distance on a raised platform protected by a perspex screen and a double hurdle of potted plants.

But it took the first 45 minutes for stewards to remove one-by-one over 120 of the protesters from the meeting at the Queen Elizabeth II conference centre in London's Westminster, before chairman Bob Bauman and chief executive Sir Richard Evans could make themselves heard above chants of "Stop Selling Hawks to Indonesia."

A spokesman for the Campaign Against the Arms Trade (CAAT) told Reuters that about 150 people had bought shares in BAe to get entry to the meeting this year, to protest about the sale of Hawk jets to Indonesia.

The remaining campaigners spent the rest of the meeting pursuing the issue with questions mainly protesting about BAe's Hawk sales to Indonesia, which CAAT alleges have been used to attack the civilian population of East Timor.
Bauman denied that there was any evidence of Hawks being used in East Timor, which would be in breach of assurances given to Britain by the Indonesian government.
"There is absolutely no evidence that has ever been submitted...to show that any of our weapons have ever been used to cause any death in Indonesia," he told shareholders.

John Weston, a BAe managing director and head of the defence business, said the company would have a fair idea if Hawks had flown into East Timor because BAe still had technical staff supporting its Hawk sales in Indonesia.
"Which is one reason why we have a good idea of where these aircraft are and what they are doing," he said.
